subject: math-ai-sl
title: School travel survey
stem: An institution has 600 members: 20% in group A, 30% in group B and 50% in group C. A researcher wants a stratified random sample of 60 members.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find the number selected from each group.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Describe how to select members within each group.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain a possible bias if the researcher surveys only people arriving before 08:00.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Identify the population and a suitable quantitative variable for a travel survey.

steps.text: Multiply the sample size by each population proportion.
Number all members in each group and use a random-number generator to choose distinct members, giving each member in that group an equal chance.
Early arrivals may have different habits from later arrivals, so some groups or behaviours may be underrepresented.
The population is all 600 institution members.
For example, one-way travel time in minutes; accept another measurable numerical travel variable.

verification.method: Independent standard-library numerical and mathematical checks
verification.notes: Stratum allocations sum to 60; reasoning checked against equal-chance sampling definitions. Rounding is to three significant figures unless otherwise specified.

Assume the population assessment scores under each method are normally distributed with equal unknown variances. Let the population mean scores be $\mu_A$ and $\mu_B$ for methods A and B respectively. Test whether the mean assessment scores differ between the methods at the 5% significance level.

| A | B |
| --- | --- |
| 15 | 19 |
| 17 | 21 |
| 18 | 20 |
| 16 | 23 |
| 19 | 22 |
| 17 | 21 |
| 20 | 24 |
| 18 | 20 |

parts.prompt: Explain why a paired t-test would be inappropriate.

steps.text: $H_1:\mu_A\ne\mu_B$.
Use an unpaired pooled two-sample t-test, with a two-sided alternative.
$t=-4.58$ using A minus B; $p=0.000426$. A reversed statistic sign is acceptable with the same two-sided p-value.
There is sufficient evidence that the population mean assessment scores differ between teaching methods A and B.
The observations are from independent samples, with no matched relationship between entries in the two columns.
